910.name: Helvetii Celts & Roman Helvetia
910.description: The Helvetii, a Celtic people, gave Switzerland its Latin name (Confoederatio Helvetica). Their attempted migration was blocked by Caesar at Bibracte (58 BCE), and the region was integrated into the Roman Empire as part of several provinces.

sub_clusters.name: Helvetii & La Tène Culture
sub_clusters.description: The Helvetii and their La Tène material culture centred on the Swiss Plateau, oppida settlements, and the decision to migrate westward that brought them into conflict with Rome.
key_events: Caesar defeats the Helvetii at the Battle of Bibracte (58 BCE)

sub_clusters.name: Roman Provinces & Aventicum
sub_clusters.description: Romanisation of Helvetia, the flourishing colony of Aventicum (Avenches) as a provincial capital, Alpine pass control, and the decline during the Migration Period.

920.name: Old Swiss Confederacy Origins
920.description: The legendary founding of the Swiss Confederacy with the Rütli Oath and Federal Charter of 1291, followed by stunning military victories against Habsburg armies that established Swiss independence.

sub_clusters.name: Federal Charter of 1291 & Early Cantons
sub_clusters.description: The Bundesbrief (Federal Charter) of 1 August 1291 uniting Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden, the William Tell legend, and the Battle of Morgarten (1315) where Swiss peasants routed a Habsburg army.
key_events: Federal Charter of the Swiss Confederacy signed (1 August 1291)
Battle of Morgarten – Swiss defeat Habsburg forces (1315)

sub_clusters.name: Confederate Expansion
sub_clusters.description: Growth of the Confederacy through the addition of Lucerne, Zürich, Bern, and other cantons, the Battle of Sempach (1386), and the conquest of Aargau from the Habsburgs.

920.name: Burgundian Wars & Swiss Military Power
920.description: The Swiss Confederacy reached the peak of its military reputation through devastating victories over Charles the Bold of Burgundy and service as Europe's most sought-after mercenaries.

sub_clusters.name: Burgundian Wars
sub_clusters.description: Swiss victories at Grandson, Morat, and Nancy (1474–1477) destroyed Burgundian power and made the Swiss pike square the most feared formation in European warfare.
key_events: Battle of Morat – Swiss Confederacy crushes Charles the Bold (1476)

sub_clusters.name: Italian Wars & Battle of Marignano
sub_clusters.description: Swiss mercenary service in the Italian Wars, brief Swiss control of Milan, and the defeat at Marignano (1515) that ended Swiss expansionism and turned the Confederacy toward neutrality.

930.name: Swiss Reformation
930.description: Switzerland was a cradle of the Protestant Reformation, with Zwingli in Zürich and Calvin in Geneva creating distinct Reformed traditions that profoundly influenced Protestant Christianity worldwide.

sub_clusters.name: Zwingli & the Zürich Reformation
sub_clusters.description: Huldrych Zwingli's reforms in Zürich, the Zürich disputations, the break with radical Anabaptists, the Kappel Wars, and Zwingli's death in battle at Kappel (1531).
key_events: Zwingli begins the Reformation in Zürich (1519)
Zwingli killed at the Battle of Kappel (1531)

sub_clusters.name: Calvin & Geneva
sub_clusters.description: John Calvin's transformation of Geneva into a model Reformed city-state, the Ecclesiastical Ordinances, the execution of Servetus, and Geneva's influence as the 'Protestant Rome' sending missionaries across Europe.

930.name: Perpetual Neutrality & Peace of Westphalia
930.description: While the Thirty Years' War devastated surrounding lands, Switzerland maintained its neutrality. The Peace of Westphalia (1648) formally recognised Swiss independence from the Holy Roman Empire and established the principle of perpetual neutrality.

sub_clusters.name: Thirty Years' War & Swiss Neutrality
sub_clusters.description: Switzerland's successful maintenance of neutrality during Europe's most destructive war, internal confessional tensions, and the formal recognition of Swiss independence at Westphalia.
key_events: Peace of Westphalia formally recognises Swiss independence from the HRE (1648)

940.name: Napoleonic Helvetic Republic
940.description: Napoleon's invasion ended the Old Confederacy and imposed the centralised Helvetic Republic (1798–1803), followed by the Act of Mediation restoring cantonal sovereignty. The Congress of Vienna (1815) guaranteed Swiss neutrality in perpetuity.

sub_clusters.name: Helvetic Republic & Act of Mediation
sub_clusters.description: French invasion, the short-lived centralised Helvetic Republic, internal resistance, and Napoleon's Act of Mediation (1803) restoring the confederal structure with six new cantons.

sub_clusters.name: Congress of Vienna & Perpetual Neutrality
sub_clusters.description: The restoration of Swiss independence and the international guarantee of Swiss perpetual neutrality at the Congress of Vienna (1815), a cornerstone of Swiss identity.
key_events: Congress of Vienna guarantees Swiss perpetual neutrality (1815)

940.name: Federal Constitution & Modern Switzerland
940.description: The brief Sonderbund War (1847) between Catholic and Protestant cantons led to the Federal Constitution of 1848, creating the modern Swiss federal state with its distinctive direct democracy, and inspiring the founding of the Red Cross.

sub_clusters.name: Sonderbund War & Federal Constitution (1848)
sub_clusters.description: Liberal reforms, the Sonderbund War (1847), and the Federal Constitution of 1848 creating a bicameral parliament, federal council, and the world's first modern federal direct democracy.
key_events: Swiss Federal Constitution establishes modern federal state (1848)

sub_clusters.name: Red Cross Founding & Industrialisation
sub_clusters.description: Henry Dunant's experience at the Battle of Solferino inspiring the founding of the Red Cross (1863), the first Geneva Convention (1864), Swiss industrialisation, railway development, and tourism.
key_events: Henry Dunant founds the International Committee of the Red Cross (1863)
First Geneva Convention establishes laws of war (1864)

950.name: Swiss Neutrality in the World Wars
950.description: Switzerland maintained armed neutrality through both World Wars, serving as a humanitarian hub and diplomatic meeting ground while facing internal linguistic tensions and controversies over its relationship with Nazi Germany.

sub_clusters.name: WWI Armed Neutrality
sub_clusters.description: General Wille's mobilisation, the Graben (linguistic divide) between francophone and germanophone Swiss, the 1918 general strike, and Switzerland's hosting of the League of Nations.

sub_clusters.name: WWII Neutrality & Controversies
sub_clusters.description: General Guisan's Réduit national defence strategy, the controversial turning away of Jewish refugees (J-stamp), Swiss banking of Nazi gold, and the moral complexities of wartime neutrality.
key_events: General Guisan's Rütli address rallying Swiss defence (1940)

960.name: Postwar Prosperity & International Hub
960.description: Switzerland's postwar development as a banking centre, seat of international organisations in Geneva, the women's suffrage struggle (federal level only in 1971), and the tortuous debate over international integration.

sub_clusters.name: Banking Centre & Cold War Role
sub_clusters.description: Swiss banking secrecy, Geneva as a hub for UN agencies and Cold War diplomacy, the Red Cross's expanded role, and controversies over dormant Holocaust-era accounts.

sub_clusters.name: Women's Suffrage & Direct Democracy
sub_clusters.description: The belated introduction of women's suffrage at the federal level (1971), Appenzell Innerrhoden forced by court to grant cantonal suffrage (1990), and the evolution of Switzerland's unique direct democracy system.
key_events: Swiss women gain federal voting rights (1971)

960.name: Contemporary Switzerland
960.description: Switzerland's careful engagement with international institutions—rejecting EEA membership (1992), joining the UN only in 2002—while confronting banking secrecy reforms, immigration debates, and its role as a global diplomatic hub.

sub_clusters.name: UN Membership & the Bilateral Path
sub_clusters.description: Rejection of EEA membership (1992), the bilateral agreements with the EU, UN membership approved by referendum (2002), banking secrecy reforms under international pressure, and the SVP's anti-immigration politics.
key_events: Switzerland joins the United Nations by referendum (2002)

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
